Vaccines work by teaching the immune system to recognize a disease before the body ever encounters it. To understand how, it helps to know what the immune system normally does. When a harmful germ enters the body, immune cells identify it as foreign and produce proteins called antibodies to neutralize it. This process takes time, which is why a first infection can make you very sick.

A vaccine gives the immune system a safe preview. It contains a harmless piece or weakened form of the germ, or instructions for making a single protein from it. The body responds just as it would to a real threat, producing antibodies and creating specialized memory cells.

These memory cells are the key to lasting protection. If the real germ appears later, the immune system recognizes it quickly and mounts a rapid, powerful response, often stopping the infection before symptoms develop. Some vaccines require booster doses to maintain this memory over time. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the disease also has a harder time spreading, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated themselves.
